commentBody: A fine gimmick that at least didn't get in the way of a pleasant solve
Very clever and a wonderful debut!
Nice debut and theme, even if it was over too quickly.

Fine debut. Nice easy Thursday (or Wednesday?). Good news and bad news (IMO) is that people will be able fill in the puzzle (and get their gold stars) without understanding the theme. Fire blanks indeed.

I was fired up to do this puzzle, so I  liked the theme which I found quite clever.  I entered some of them without catching on to the trick, but once I had enough crosses to get the revealer I raced to fill in the rest.  My favorite was LAMBASTED for put under ——.
Great fun!

Congratulations on your debut! This was a well thought out theme and a nice grid. I will probably not be the only one to wish it had been clued at a bit of a higher level and wonder if this weren’t better as a Wednesday theme. I say that because once you get the theme (took me a little bit, but not too long) then it becomes a themeless, and not a hard one at that. But none of that is up to you. It was still a great idea and a cute revealer. My only nit is “fireball” for COMET. Comets are made of ice and aren’t on fire. METEOR is more accurate but of course that doesn’t fit there; but they aren’t symmetric revealers so it didn’t need to be 5 letters. I’m going to just assume this is the metaphoric meaning of COMET, like “the entertainer’s MEGAHIT streaked to the top of the charts like a COMET”. Or maybe the reindeer was a bit of a fireball. Still, Frances may have something to say about that. My latest Crosshare puzzle is in; it’s a bit of a loose theme and breaks an unwritten rule about revealer placement. But, I think it’s pretty fun, has my favorite title of any of my puzzles, and is a pangram. https://crosshare.org/crosswords/t0ZW6f6CbLMNHFp3taeM/put-up-your-dooks
Really enjoyed this puzzle,  made me smile!   Thank you!

Didn’t we just have a puzzle where the blanks were in the grid and not the clues?

I don’t get flustered when doing a Thursday and I don’t immediately catch onto the trick. I just work around it until something fills itself in. Watching a playoff game (can you say “leadoff homer*”?) at the same time didn’t help. 

My time was slower than usual, but it was because of the conditions I was working under. Once I saw the trick, things moved quickly. 

* On the very first pitch of the game
Nice puzzle. Solved it without any insight into the twist.
Solved this low-key Thursday puzzle with a minimum of HOOPLA. Just one, in fact.

To those who are getting acquainted with NYT puzzles.  This is a fair Thursday.  You have to figure out the blank word that is missing from the clue, but that word isn’t the answer - it’s merely the rest of the clue. 

This is a mental workout that takes time to spot and understand. A good tip is if you see something you don’t quite understand, keep solving until you can see one of the answers start to appear.  Then from there you can reverse engineer the word play used for a particular puzzle.  This is also key for solving rebus clues. 

Remember, crosswords are like life, and things aren’t always as they pleas.

Anyone else google “comet ball”?
Haha, I was firing blanks on that one.

(There apparently is a juggling doodad called a comet ball.)
Oh what a lovely Thursday. Absolutely loved the theme. Nicely done, designer! Wonderful debut! Congrats!
Was wondering what the trick was all the way to the end. Nicely done!
LAMBASTED was the last word I filled in because it made no sense to me, and yet I got the happy music anyway.
Nice puzzle but, to be fair, calling a COMET a fireball is a bit far since it’s actually an ice ball that releases gas as the sun heats it up. So it’s about as far from a fireball as you can get.

how do you comment without giving away the theme?  no spoilers!   this puzzle was Fire in every way the reveal is an all time classic thanks McKay bravo on an exception debut. beautiful puzzle - this is why we love Thursdays puzzles. kudos all around!

Another puzzle where I just circled the grid, guessing what might be right, skipping answers that seemed too iffy, but keeping them in mind (e.g., LOADSUP), and finally understanding what the blanks represented.  Looking things up wasn't wasn't necessary  because that seldom helps except with proper names I'm clueless about, and the puzzle was free of those.

What it all added up to for me was a tightly constructed, cleverly clued debut, one to be proud of (a Thursday, no less!).  Congratulations, McKay Fritz.

for nitpickers - honors in Astronomy grad Hunter College NYC chiming in - a Fireball means meteor or Comet as it passes through space or the atmosphere of another planet - it refers not to Fire but to the 'tail' which is literally FIRE.  the slow burn off of the material of the comet or meteor as it hurdles through space.

Congratulations, McKay Fritz, on your crossword debut! Nicely done, even if it was not quite as tricky as I like to see on Thursday. (But that’s on the editors; to me, this would have been more appropriately placed on a Wednesday.) I was interested to read your shout-out to the people who publish the Ingrid puzzle construction site. I’ve not tried that one, but I have had some luck with Crosserville, another free web-based construction option. I’d urge anyone who is interested in construction to give it a try. There are lots of good resources, including the NYT series on “How to Make a Crossword Puzzle” and Patrick Berry’s comprehensive “Crossword Constructor’s Handbook.” https://www.nytimes.com/2018/09/14/crosswords/how-to-make-a-crossword-puzzle-the-series.html https://aframegames.com/store/?download=21 Two great things about crossword construction as a hobby as compared to knitting, painting, pottery or whatever* are that the finished product takes up only disk space! And you might even get paid for it! *Let me be clear that I am not knocking any craft-making hobbies. I know lots of people who do that sort of thing and that’s great. It’s just not for me.

I haven't read all the comments yet, so am I the first to point out the Scott Joplin said that ragtime music should never be played fast? I think Joshua Rifkin may be credited with the rediscovery of that principle. https://youtu.be/Rad6UvoGHV8?si=1QnJA_o30n-k34Ha I was on the right track for 51A, but I went for pennibs before ERASERS. Nice misdirect there. Similarly, I thought that [Wheel that comes apart easily?] might be a novel cluing for Oreo before I saw that it had to be BRIE. Thanks for a fun Thursday!

Although *Joplin: Complete Rags* (Schirmer ed.) is sitting on the piano, a mere four feet away from where I solved this puzzle, I resisted the temptation to get up and check what key the "Maple Leaf Rag" was in. I knew it was *something*-flat; Joplin, like most romantic composers, favored the flat keys. Here's the 1970 recording of "Maple Leaf Rag" by American musicologist Joshua Rifkin, who was, perhaps, single-handedly responsible for the "Joplin revival." (Rifkin's other major area of study was the choral compositions of J.S. Bach; his Bach performances and recordings are still controversial.): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e10k9QIjTU4&list=RDe10k9QIjTU4&start_radio=1 It's worth repeating Joplin's famous admonition to solvers: "Do not solve this puzzle fast. It is never right to solve crosswords fast."

Well, I love riddles.  One reason is that the good ones almost always stump me.  My brain just seems to have a hard time doing that kind of thinking.

Still, my persistent brain works and works at trying to solve good riddles, and when, finally, I uncle, and receive the answer, it brings a huge aha because I put so much effort into it – looked at it from so many angles. I feel I’ve been gotten good and fair, and it’s a sweet wow experience all around.

And thus today, with the Big Riddle as to what went into the blanks.  Oh, I worked hard.  I refused to uncover the revealer, and tried every which way to crack the riddle.  And then, when the grid was nearly filled in, the answer hit me.  Well, even better than being gotten good is a successful riddle-crack.

Yes, I will be walking a bit taller today.  Thank you, McKay, for coming up with a simple and elegant concept that drove me mad for a bit, and brought a huge "Yes!!!" Congratulations on your debut, and more like this please!

Although there is no doubt that ABACI are 16A [Ancient calculation tools], it is also true that they are still in use today.

From Wikipedia:

"In the ancient world, abacuses were a practical calculating tool. They were widely used in Europe as late as the 17th century, but fell out of use with the rise of decimal notation[5] and algorismic methods. Although calculators and computers are commonly used today instead of abacuses, abacuses remain in everyday use in some countries. The abacus has an advantage of not requiring a writing implement and paper (needed for algorism) or an electric power source. Merchants, traders, and clerks in some parts of Eastern Europe, Russia, China, and Africa use abacuses. The abacus remains in common use as a scoring system in non-electronic table games. Others may use an abacus due to visual impairment that prevents the use of a calculator.[2] The abacus is still used to teach the fundamentals of mathematics to children in many countries such as Japan[6] and China.[7]"

I know a young student who just received her bachelor's degree from a great university as a pre-med student with great grades. She wants to study for the MCAT to continue to medical school. She told me that the MCATs do not allow use of calculators at the test. She seemed to have no idea how to do simple calculations without her calculator. Pity. I asked her: "What is ten percent of 150?"  and she was lost. What a world!

Fun fact:  Irving Berlin, who never studied piano formally, preferred to play on the black keys as much as possible. Anyone who has tried it realizes that it is a LOT more comfortable and natural feeling. Dunno if Scott Joplin shared this quirk, but A flat spends a lot of time on the black keys!

When I first played these, it was a discovery seeing that Joplin marked tempos for many of them as "Not fast." Playing them that way revealed a depth, sadness, and contemplativeness that popular recordings did not. I fell in love with them.

On a completely different note: I have a rant. I wasted a half hour today trying to follow Google's suggestions to get the puzzles to load. I was logged into my subscription and could bring up News and Cooking in my browser on laptop and see the puzzles on my phone app, but in my browser a blank space yawned where the crosswords and archives should be. My browser auto-updates so I didn't think that was the issue. But once I decided to ignore all the confident Gemini suggestions and just think a moment, I checked and saw the auto-update had stalled. Once I fixed that, everything was fine.
